Entity mapping: @OneToMany / @ManyToOne with cascade and orphanRemoval

mappedBy marks Order.items as the inverse side, so the FK is managed by OrderItem.order. cascade = ALL saves and deletes items along with their order. orphanRemoval deletes an item from the database when it is removed from the list. Don't use Lombok @Data on entities, because the generated equals/hashCode/toString walk the lazy associations.
Derived query methods
Spring builds the JPQL from the method name. Keywords include And, Or, Between, LessThan, Like, Containing, In, IsNull, Top/First and OrderBy. Switch to @Query once a name gets unreadable.
@Query with JPQL and native SQL (and @Modifying)

JPQL works with entity and field names and is portable across databases. Native queries use table and column names and can use features specific to one database. Bulk updates need @Modifying and skip the persistence context, which is why the code clears it.
Projections: interface-based and DTO constructor queries

Projections fetch fewer columns and return read-only objects that are never managed or dirty-checked, so they are cheaper. A constructor expression needs the fully qualified class name. Spring Data 3 can also map a JPQL tuple into a record directly.
Fixing N+1 with JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph

Don't use JOIN FETCH on a collection together with pagination. Hibernate then pages in memory and logs warning HHH90003004. In that case, fetch a page of IDs first, then fetch those orders with their items. You can't JOIN FETCH two List bags at once (MultipleBagFetchException), so use a Set or separate queries.
Pagination with Pageable, and a separate count query
Page runs an extra COUNT query, and Slice doesn't. Give a custom countQuery for complex joins. On very large tables, use keyset (seek) pagination such as where id > :lastId instead of large offsets.
Optimistic locking with @Version

When another transaction has already changed the row, the update matches 0 rows and Spring throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException. Retry it or return 409 Conflict. @Retryable comes from spring-retry and needs @EnableRetry. Optimistic locking fits when conflicts are rare. Pessimistic locking fits hot rows.
Auditing with @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate and @CreatedBy
Spring fills these fields automatically on persist and update. Hibernate's own @CreationTimestamp and @UpdateTimestamp do the same for timestamps, but they don't support "by user".
Specifications for dynamic filters

Specifications wrap the Criteria API in small predicates you can combine. That fits search screens with optional filters, so you don't need a separate query method for every combination. Specification.allOf arrived in Spring Data 3.0, and older versions chain where(a).and(b). Querydsl is the alternative.
Batch insert tips

Hibernate can't batch inserts for IDENTITY IDs, because it needs each generated key straight away. Use a SEQUENCE with a pooled allocation size, or JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate. Flushing and clearing every N rows keeps the persistence context from growing without limit.
@ManyToMany (students and courses) with helper methods, and when to use a join entity

Keep both sides in sync with helper methods, because JPA only writes what the owning side (the one without mappedBy) contains. Use a Set: with a List, Hibernate deletes and re-inserts all join rows on a change. Never use cascade = REMOVE on many-to-many, since deleting a student would delete shared courses. As soon as the relationship needs its own data, replace it with a join entity and two @ManyToOne links.
Composite primary key with @EmbeddedId, and value objects with @Embeddable

A composite id class must implement equals/hashCode and be Serializable. Records work well for simple embeddable value objects such as Address (Hibernate 6.2+), while a mutable class is the safer choice for an id that @MapsId fills in. @IdClass is the alternative that keeps the id fields directly on the entity. Many teams avoid composite keys altogether: add a surrogate id and a unique constraint on the natural pair, which keeps repositories and URLs simple.
Inheritance mapping: SINGLE_TABLE vs JOINED vs TABLE_PER_CLASS vs @MappedSuperclass

Strategy | Tables | Pros | Cons
SINGLE_TABLE (default) | One table + discriminator | Fastest, polymorphic queries need no joins | Subclass columns must be nullable
JOINED | Parent table + one per subclass | Normalised, NOT NULL constraints possible | Joins on every polymorphic read
TABLE_PER_CLASS | One full table per concrete class | No joins for one subtype | Polymorphic queries use UNION; no IDENTITY ids
@MappedSuperclass | Only subclass tables | Share common fields (id, audit columns) | Not an entity: no polymorphic queries
Default to SINGLE_TABLE for small hierarchies, JOINED when subclasses have many required fields, and @MappedSuperclass when you only want to reuse fields (like the Auditable base class).
Soft delete: @SQLDelete with @SQLRestriction (Hibernate 6)

Soft delete keeps data for auditing and undo, which is common in healthcare and finance. Trade-offs: unique constraints must include the deleted flag (or use a partial or generated column), every query pays the extra filter (index it), and the restriction does not apply to native queries. For a full history of changes, Hibernate Envers (@Audited) is the better tool.
LazyInitializationException: why it happens and how to fix it

A lazy association is a proxy that needs an open persistence context to load. Once the transaction (and session) closes, touching it throws. Fix it by fetching deliberately (join fetch, entity graph, DTO projection) or by mapping inside the service transaction. Avoid the anti-patterns: switching to EAGER, or hibernate.enable_lazy_load_no_trans. Spring Boot leaves Open Session In View on by default (with a warning), which hides the problem but keeps a DB connection for the whole request and causes N+1 queries in the view layer.
Map enums and custom types: @Enumerated(STRING) and AttributeConverter

The default EnumType.ORDINAL stores the position, so inserting a new constant in the middle silently corrupts existing data. Always use STRING, or a converter when the database needs a short code. Converters are also handy for encrypting a column, or storing a small list or JSON value (Hibernate 6 also supports @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON) for JSON columns).
equals() and hashCode() for JPA entities

A generated id is null before persist, so a hash based on the id would change after saving and the entity would be "lost" inside a HashSet. The usual answers are: compare by id but return a constant hashCode (above), or use an immutable natural key such as ISBN for both. Don't use Lombok's @Data or @EqualsAndHashCode on entities: they include lazy collections, which can trigger loading and infinite recursion. Use instanceof or getClass() through a getter because the other object may be a proxy.
Test a repository with @DataJpaTest

@DataJpaTest loads only the persistence layer and wraps each test in a transaction that is rolled back. By default it swaps in an embedded database; Replace.NONE plus Testcontainers tests against the real engine, which matters for native queries. Call flush() and clear() before asserting, otherwise you are only reading objects from the persistence context and not testing the mapping or the query.
persist() vs merge() vs Spring Data save()

| em.persist(e) | em.merge(e) | repository.save(e)
Input | New entity | Detached (or new) entity | Either
Return | void: e itself becomes managed | A managed copy; e stays detached | The managed instance; use the return value
Detached input | Error: "detached entity passed to persist" | Copies its state onto the managed row | Calls merge
SQL | INSERT at flush | SELECT if not loaded, then UPDATE/INSERT at flush | persist if isNew() (id null or version null), else merge
Interview tip: with an assigned (not generated) id, save() thinks the entity is not new and calls merge, causing an extra SELECT. Implement Persistable or add a @Version field to fix it. And a managed entity needs no save() at all: dirty checking writes the change.
findById() vs getReferenceById()

| findById(id) | getReferenceById(id)
Hits the DB | Yes, immediately (unless already in the context) | No, returns a lazy proxy
Missing row | Optional.empty() | EntityNotFoundException later, on first field access
Return type | Optional<T> | T (proxy)
Best for | Reading and showing data | Setting a foreign key without loading the parent
Rule of thumb: read with findById; link with getReferenceById. Never return a reference proxy to the web layer.
FetchType.LAZY vs EAGER: what are the defaults and which should you use?

| LAZY | EAGER
Default for | @OneToMany, @ManyToMany | @ManyToOne, @OneToOne
Loads related data | On first access | Always, with the owner
Main risk | N+1 queries, LazyInitializationException | Loads data you never use; N+1 in JPQL queries too
Can you override per query? | Yes: JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph | Not reliably: an EAGER mapping stays eager
Rule of thumb: make every association LAZY (set fetch = LAZY on @ManyToOne explicitly) and fetch what each use case needs with JOIN FETCH or an entity graph.
Page vs Slice vs List as a repository return type

| Page<T> | Slice<T> | List<T> with Pageable
Queries | Data + a COUNT query | Data only (fetches size + 1 rows) | Data only
Knows total pages | Yes | No, only hasNext() | No
Cost on big tables | COUNT can be slow | Cheap | Cheap
UI fit | Numbered pages "1 2 3 … 40" | "Load more" / infinite scroll | Internal batch jobs
Rule of thumb: Page only when the screen really shows a total; otherwise Slice. For very deep pages, keyset pagination (WHERE id > :lastId) beats OFFSET of any kind.
Optimistic vs pessimistic locking

| Optimistic (@Version) | Pessimistic (@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE))
How | UPDATE … WHERE id = ? AND version = ? | SELECT … FOR UPDATE
Conflict found | At flush: OptimisticLockException | Never: the second transaction waits
Blocking | None | Other writers block until commit
Deadlock risk | No | Yes, lock rows in a fixed order
Best for | Rare conflicts, long user edits (forms) | Hot rows with frequent conflicts: stock, balances
Rule of thumb: default to @Version and return 409 Conflict (or retry) on failure; use a pessimistic lock in a short transaction when conflicts are common and retries would be costly.
